originalTitle: Surprisingly complex waves reveal the brain's inner workings
content:
I get out of bed. I walk through the dimly lit hallway, thinking of what’s in my fridge and what I should have for breakfast. With no real effort, I’ve navigated my environment, accessed my memory, and assessed the energetic state of my body, all in the space of a few seconds. How is the brain able to do this?

Partly by harnessing electricity. The brain spends about half of its energetic resources maintaining the electrochemical gradients that keep neurons poised and ready to fire at a moment’s notice. This gives the brain an extraordinary level of flexibility in responding to the demands of everyday life. The collective electrical activity of many neurons can be seen as waves propagating through the brain from one region to the next, like the raised arms of enthusiastic spectators at a football game.

New lines of research are revealing that these waves are more complex than previously known. Typically measured by electrodes, they have been identified as basic planar waves: simply structured oscillations in neural activity. Neuroscientists have traditionally interpreted this as a bit like the sound of the brain’s engine revving, little more than a sign that it’s working. However, emerging evidence in humans and animals suggests that traveling waves play a central role in how the brain functions.

“The work coming out is moving this from ‘Are they relevant?’ to ‘This is a major motif of how the cortex processes information,’” said Earl K. Miller , a cognitive neuroscientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

In a study published in April 2026 in Nature Communications , neuroscientists measured traveling waves of neural activity and observed a menagerie: source waves that appear to emanate from one location, sink waves that converge on a spot, and vortexlike spiral waves. The team, which included Joshua Jacobs and Anup Das from the University of Chicago, found that different behavioral tasks were associated with distinct wave patterns.

Joshua Jacobs and Anup Das were part of a team that observed complex patterns of brain waves using intracranial electrodes.

Neurons can change connections with their neighbors over time, but this usually happens on the scale of days or months. Behavior, however, needs to adapt in seconds. A significant number of neuroscientists now believe these large-scale wave patterns may help to reorganize the brain in real time to meet the behavioral demands of waking life.

“Even if the traveling wave was just the result of neurons firing, like the sound of the engine, it still tells us something very interesting about the brain based on what the person is doing,” Jacobs said. “If you see a sound moving in a direction across your engine, it means something in your engine is directionally organized.”

As far back as the 1920s , neuroscientists have been measuring the brain’s oscillating electrical activity with electrodes on the surface of the scalp via electroencephalography (EEG). When we pay attention, remember, or sleep, the large-scale frequency of the brain’s electrical activity changes. These various oscillations are commonly known as alpha, beta, gamma, and theta waves, and are measured in hertz.

But recording electrical activity from outside the skull limits the fidelity of the information you can gather. Jacobs’ lab specializes in intracranial brain recordings. People with severe epilepsy may have had electrodes placed inside their brain to help locate the source of their seizures. With roughly 100 electrodes placed in a particular brain region, and with permission from the patient, Jacobs and his team are able to capture high-resolution data — across both space and time — as the participants perform various thinking tasks.

Jacobs and his collaborator Uma Mohan , who is now a neuroengineer at the National Institutes of Health, were part of a team that used this technique to observe brain activity during memory tasks. In a study published in Nature Human Behavior in 2024, they described waves moving in opposite directions across the brain’s outermost region, the cortex. “They either go back to front or front to back across the brain,” Jacobs said.

Jacobs said a good way to understand this result is to think of the waves as showing the direction of information propagation. Visual regions are in the back, and the prefrontal cortex, the “higher-level” memory region, is at the front. If you’re paying attention to what you are looking at, signals are traveling backward from receptors in your eyes to the visual cortex, and then forward into the rest of the brain via the wave to form a memory. “The signature of that is to see waves going from the back of the brain to the front,” Jacobs said.

“We thought that was a way the brain was exploiting this organization to switch between encoding and recall memory functions on a rapid timescale, depending on what you need your brain to be supporting,” Mohan explained.

The 2026 research from Jacobs and Das complicated this picture. It showed that these waves can take on much more diverse shapes, patterns, and ripples, far beyond those created by simple up-and-down and back-to-front movement.

In the experiment, the team asked participants to perform two memory tasks. The first was a simple verbal memory exercise, in which they had to recall words they had seen on a screen. The second was a more complex spatial task: They navigated a virtual environment and had to recall the locations of objects they encountered.

With the high-resolution method, Jacobs and Das observed two new classes of waves in awake humans for the first time. One, emanating from an area of the cortex, was a concentric wave, like the ripples from a pebble dropped into a lake, or the reverse, in which waves converged on one region. The other was a rotating spiral wave traveling in a clockwise or counterclockwise direction, like a hurricane or a flushing toilet.

chineseTitle: 令人惊讶的复杂波揭示了大脑的内部运作
chineseContent:
我起床了。我穿过昏暗的走廊，想着冰箱里有什么以及早餐应该吃什么。我不需要付出任何努力，就可以在几秒钟内浏览我的环境、访问我的记忆并评估我身体的能量状态。大脑是如何做到这一点的呢？

部分通过利用电力。大脑花费大约一半的能量资源来维持电化学梯度，使神经元保持平衡并准备好随时放电。这使大脑在应对日常生活需求方面具有非凡的灵活性。许多神经元的集体电活动可以被视为通过大脑从一个区域传播到下一个区域的电波，就像足球比赛中热情的观众举起的手臂一样。

新的研究表明这些波比之前已知的更加复杂。通常通过电极测量，它们被识别为基本平面波：神经活动中简单结构的振荡。神经科学家传统上将其解释为有点像大脑引擎运转的声音，只不过是它正在工作的迹象。然而，人类和动物身上的新证据表明，行波在大脑功能中发挥着核心作用。

麻省理工学院的认知神经科学家厄尔·K·米勒 (Earl K. Miller) 表示：“即将开展的工作正在将这个问题从‘它们相关吗？’转变为‘这是皮层如何处理信息的主要主题’。”

在《自然通讯》2026 年 4 月发表的一项研究中，神经科学家测量了神经活动的行波，并观察到了一个动物园：似乎从一个位置发出的源波、汇聚在一个点上的沉波以及漩涡状的螺旋波。该团队包括芝加哥大学的约书亚·雅各布斯和阿努普·达斯，他们发现不同的行为任务与不同的波浪模式相关。

Joshua Jacobs 和 Anup Das 所在的团队使用颅内电极观察复杂的脑电波模式。

随着时间的推移，神经元可以改变与邻居的连接，但这通常会在几天或几个月的时间内发生。然而，行为需要在几秒钟内适应。现在，大量神经科学家相信这些大规模的波模式可能有助于实时重组大脑，以满足清醒生活的行为需求。

雅各布斯说：“即使行波只是神经元放电的结果，就像发动机的声音一样，它仍然可以根据人正在做的事情告诉我们一些关于大脑的非常有趣的事情。” “如果你看到声音沿着引擎的方向移动，则意味着引擎中的某些东西是有方向组织的。”

早在 20 世纪 20 年代，神经科学家就一直在通过脑电图 (EEG) 使用头皮表面的电极来测量大脑的振荡电活动。当我们集中注意力、记忆力或睡眠时，大脑电活动的频率会发生大规模变化。这些不同的振荡通常称为 α、β、γ 和 θ 波，以赫兹为单位测量。

但是从头骨外部记录电活动限制了您可以收集的信息的保真度。雅各布斯的实验室专门研究颅内脑记录。患有严重癫痫症的人可能在大脑内放置了电极，以帮助找到癫痫发作的根源。在获得患者许可的情况下，雅各布斯和他的团队将大约 100 个电极放置在特定的大脑区域，当参与者执行各种思维任务时，他们能够跨空间和时间捕获高分辨率数据。

雅各布斯和他的合作者乌玛·莫汉（Uma Mohan）现在是美国国立卫生研究院的神经工程师，他们所在的团队使用这种技术来观察记忆任务期间的大脑活动。在 2024 年《自然人类行为》杂志上发表的一项研究中，他们描述了大脑最外层区域（皮层）沿相反方向移动的波。 “它们要么从后到前，要么从前到后穿过大脑，”雅各布斯说。

雅各布斯说，理解这一结果的一个好方法是将波视为显示信息传播的方向。视觉区域位于后面，前额皮质（“高级”记忆区域）位于前面。如果你正在注意你所看到的东西，信号就会从你眼睛里的受体向后传播到视觉皮层，然后通过电波向前传播到大脑的其他部分，形成记忆。 “其特征是看到电波从大脑后部传到前部，”雅各布斯说。

“我们认为这是大脑利用这个组织在编码和回忆记忆功能之间快速切换的一种方式，具体取决于你需要大脑支持什么，”莫汉解释道。

Jacobs 和 Das 的 2026 年研究使情况变得更加复杂。它表明，这些波浪可以呈现出更加多样化的形状、图案和涟漪，远远超出简单的上下和从后到前运动所产生的效果。

在实验中，研究小组要求参与者执行两项记忆任务。第一个是简单的言语记忆练习，他们必须回忆在屏幕上看到的单词。第二个是更复杂的空间任务：他们在虚拟环境中导航并必须回忆他们遇到的物体的位置。

利用高分辨率方法，雅各布斯和达斯首次在清醒的人类身上观察到了两种新的波。其中一种是从大脑皮层的某个区域发出的，是同心波，就像一颗卵石落入湖中产生的涟漪，或者相反，波会聚在一个区域。另一种是顺时针或逆时针方向传播的旋转螺旋波，就像飓风或冲水马桶。
